pos: n. (Griffith Jones, 1683–1761, rector of Llanddowror, founder of the Welsh circulating schools)
etymology: Welsh Gruffudd, strong grip; Jones, patronymic from John.
biblical_def: Griffith Jones was rector of Llanddowror in Carmarthenshire and the man who taught Wales to read. Beginning about 1731 he organized circulating schools: a master would settle in a parish for three months in the slack season between harvest and sowing, teach adults and children together to read Welsh and to say the catechism, and then move on, the parish clergy carrying on what was begun. By his death some three thousand two hundred schools had been held and perhaps two hundred thousand people taught, in a nation of under half a million. He was no separatist and remained in the established church, but Howell Harris and Daniel Rowland were both under his influence, and the Welsh revival came to a literate people because of him. Psa 119:130 is the whole programme: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” Act 17:11 explains why reading mattered, since a people who cannot search the Scriptures must take their religion second-hand.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a catechism as a form of instruction by means of questions and answers; and literature, as learning; acquaintance with letters or books.
webster_full: CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
CIR'CULATING, ppr. Passing from place to place, from person to person, or from hand to hand.
INSTRUC'TION, n. The act of teaching or informing the understanding; information; the act of communicating knowledge.
scriptures: The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: Two hundred thousand Welsh people learned to read in schools that lasted three months and then moved on.
corruption_paragraphs: The design is worth studying because it fitted the people rather than the institution. Jones did not wait for buildings, endowments or a national system; he used the agricultural calendar, taught in the people's own language when the fashionable opinion held that Welsh should be allowed to die, and taught adults alongside their children. Psa 119:130 promises light to the simple from the entrance of God's words, and Jones took the promise as an operating instruction.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that literacy in the vernacular Scriptures is a missionary work and not merely a social improvement. 2Ti 3:16 makes all Scripture profitable for doctrine, reproof, correction and instruction, and a profit no one can read is no profit. Where churches today outsource teaching to professionals and assume their people will absorb doctrine by attendance, Isa 8:20's test cannot be applied by the congregation at all.

pos: n. (Howell Harris, 1714–1773, Welsh exhorter, co-founder of Welsh Calvinistic Methodism, founder of the Trevecca family)
biblical_def: Howell Harris was converted in 1735 at Talgarth while taking communion, and within weeks was exhorting his neighbours in farmhouses across Breconshire. He was never ordained; the bishops refused him three times, and he worked for nearly forty years as a lay exhorter, organizing converts into societies with appointed leaders — the structure Welsh Calvinistic Methodism was built on. He travelled relentlessly, was stoned and beaten repeatedly, and met Daniel Rowland in 1737 to form a partnership of exhorter and preacher that carried the Welsh awakening. A quarrel over doctrine and over Harris's association with Madam Sidney Griffith split them from 1750 to 1763. Afterwards he withdrew to Trevecca and gathered a Christian community of about a hundred families living and working in common. Act 8:4 describes his ministry's form. Mat 9:38 its necessity. Rom 10:15 the question of sending that his lack of orders kept raising.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an exhorter as one who exhorts or encourages; and a society, as a number of persons united for mutual benefit.
webster_full: EXHORT'ER, n. One who exhorts or encourages; in some churches, one who is licensed to exhort, but not to preach.
SOCI'ETY, n. A number of persons united, either for government or for mutual benefit or religious edification.
ITIN'ERANT, a. Passing or traveling from place to place; not settled.
scriptures: Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
Mat 9:38
Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.
And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!

But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.
corruption_summary: The bishops would not ordain him and he spent forty years preaching anyway, which is a question the church has never settled quietly.
corruption_paragraphs: Harris raises the hard case. The New Testament requires that preachers be sent (Rom 10:15), and the sending is ordinarily by churches through ordination; yet the established church of his day refused to send any man who preached the new birth with urgency. He answered by exhorting rather than administering the ordinances, which was a real restraint and not a fiction: he never baptized and never presided at the Table.

The modern corruption pulls both ways. One side treats ordination as a formality that gifted men may ignore, which produces unaccountable ministries; the other treats it as a guild licence that may be withheld from any man whose zeal is inconvenient. Act 20:24 shows Paul counting his life not dear so that he might finish his course and the ministry which he had received of the Lord Jesus — received, note, and not seized. The principle to recover is that the church ought to be ordaining the men God is plainly using.

roots_lines: Greek euaggelizo (G2097) — to preach good tidings; Acts 8:4.

“that he will send forth labourers into his harvest” (Mat 9:38) — the prayer he was an answer to.
“the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus” (Act 20:24) — received, not seized.

pos: n. (Daniel Rowland, 1711–1790, curate of Llangeitho, the greatest preacher of the Welsh revival)
etymology: Hebrew Daniyyel, God is my judge; Rowland, Germanic, famous land.
biblical_def: Daniel Rowland was curate of Llangeitho in Cardiganshire, converted under Griffith Jones' preaching about 1735 while still in orders and still, by his own later account, a law-preacher who terrified his hearers without offering them Christ. He learned the gospel, and for fifty years Llangeitho drew thousands on communion Sundays from every part of Wales, walking days to get there. He was never given a living of his own and in 1763 was stripped even of his curacy; he preached on in a barn built for him by the people. Contemporaries who heard both him and Whitefield thought Rowland the greater preacher. His ministry was settled where Harris's was itinerant, and the two together are the shape of the Welsh awakening. 2Ti 4:2 commanded the persistence. Rom 1:16 is the turn his preaching took when he stopped preaching only the law: the gospel “is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a curate as a clergyman employed to perform the duties of another; and eloquence, as the art of speaking with fluency and elegance, so as to persuade.
webster_full: CU'RATE, n. A clergyman employed to perform the duties of another, or in a parish church which has no incumbent.
EL'OQUENCE, n. Oratory; the act or art of speaking well, or with fluency and elegance; the power of speaking with eloquence.
COMMU'NION, n. Fellowship; the act of partaking of the Lord's supper.
scriptures: Rom 1:16
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness;
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
corruption_summary: He spent years terrifying his parish with the law and then learned the gospel, and Wales came to Llangeitho to hear it.
corruption_paragraphs: Rowland's early ministry is the useful part of his story. He was orthodox, serious, forceful and wrong, because he preached sin and judgement without the remedy, and his hearers were left in despair that produced no life. Rom 1:16 is the correction: it is the gospel, not the law, that is the power of God unto salvation. A pulpit that only convicts has done half a surgeon's work and left the patient open.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The present-day form of the error is reversed and more common: comfort without conviction, a gospel announced to people who have not been shown their need. 1Co 1:23 is the content either way, Christ crucified, which is both the offence and the only remedy. Act 20:27 requires the whole counsel of God, and the whole counsel includes both halves of what Rowland eventually preached.
roots_lines: Greek euaggelion (G2098) — the gospel, good news; Romans 1:16.
Greek kerusso (G2784) — to preach, to herald; 2 Timothy 4:2.
usage: “it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth” (Rom 1:16) — the turn at Llangeitho.
“Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) — fifty years in one village.
“all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27) — law and gospel both.

pos: n. (Llangeitho, a village in Cardiganshire, Wales; the centre of Daniel Rowland's ministry and of the Welsh Calvinistic Methodist revival)
etymology: Welsh llan, a church enclosure, with the name of the sixth-century saint Ceitho.
biblical_def: Llangeitho is a small village in the Aeron valley which, for most of the eighteenth century, was the spiritual capital of Wales. Daniel Rowland served the parish church there and, after his licence was withdrawn in 1763, preached in a barn-chapel the people built. On the monthly communion Sundays crowds came from Anglesey, Pembrokeshire and the border counties, walking for two or three days, so that observers reckoned two thousand communicants and far more hearers in a parish of a few hundred souls. The Welsh word gorfoledd, rejoicing, attached itself to the singing that broke out there. The place has no natural advantages whatever — no road, no town, no patron — which is the point. Psa 126:6 describes the traffic: he that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall come again with rejoicing. Zec 4:6 explains how a hamlet becomes a capital.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a village as a small assemblage of houses, less than a town; and pilgrimage, a long journey, particularly to some place deemed sacred.
webster_full: VIL'LAGE, n. A small assemblage of houses, less than a town or city, and inhabited chiefly by farmers and other laboring people.
PIL'GRIMAGE, n. A long journey, particularly a journey to some place deemed sacred, for the purpose of devotion.
CONGREGA'TION, n. A collection or assemblage of separate things; an assembly of persons met for the worship of God.
scriptures: He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.
Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
Psa 84:7
They go from strength to strength, every one of them in Zion appeareth before God.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
corruption_summary: People walked three days across Wales to a barn in a village with no road, for a communion service.
corruption_paragraphs: The pilgrimage to Llangeitho was not to a shrine, and the distinction matters. Nothing was venerated there; there was no relic, no holy well, no miracle-working image. People walked because a man was preaching Christ and because the Lord's Table was administered to a gathered church. Act 2:42 names the four things they came for, and all four are ordinary means of grace available, in principle, in any parish.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. It poses a question instead. The ordinary means have not changed and the appetite has. Psa 84:7 speaks of going from strength to strength on the way to appear before God in Zion, and the walking Welsh were a commentary on it. Zec 4:6 forbids us to explain the phenomenon by Rowland's eloquence alone; it was not by might, nor by power.
roots_lines: Hebrew rinnah (H7440) — a shout of joy, rejoicing; Psalm 126:6.
usage: “shall doubtless come again with rejoicing” (Psa 126:6) — the road home from Llangeitho.
“Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit” (Zec 4:6) — a village with no road.
“in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42) — what they walked three days for.

pos: n. (Thomas Charles, 1755–1814, of Bala, organizer of Welsh Sunday schools and a founder of the British and Foreign Bible Society)
etymology: Aramaic Te'oma, a twin; Charles, Germanic Karl, a free man.
biblical_def: Thomas Charles was an Oxford-trained clergyman driven out of three curacies for his evangelical preaching, who settled at Bala in Merionethshire and gave the rest of his life to teaching Wales. He extended Griffith Jones' circulating-school idea into permanent Sunday schools for all ages, wrote a Welsh scriptural dictionary and catechisms, and in 1811 reluctantly presided over the ordination of Welsh Calvinistic Methodist ministers, which made the connexion a denomination. He is best remembered for a Welsh Bible shortage: Mary Jones, a weaver's daughter of fifteen, walked twenty-five miles barefoot to Bala with six years' savings to buy one, and Charles had none to sell. Carrying the case to London in 1802 he asked why there should not be a society for the whole world, and the British and Foreign Bible Society was founded in 1804. Isa 55:11 is its charter. Psa 119:130 is what Mary Jones wanted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a Bible society as an association formed for the purpose of distributing the Scriptures; and a Sunday school, as a school for instruction on the Sabbath.
webster_full: BI'BLE, n. THE BOOK, by way of eminence; the sacred volume, in which are contained the revelations of God.
SO'CIETY, n. A number of persons united for mutual benefit or for the promotion of some object.
DISTRIBU'TION, n. The act of dividing among a number; a dealing out in parts or portions.
scriptures: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it.
corruption_summary: A girl walked twenty-five miles for a Bible that was not there, and a society was founded to make sure it would be.
corruption_paragraphs: The Mary Jones story is told so often as a children's tale that its argument is missed. The scarcity was not accidental: Welsh-language Scripture had low commercial value and no patron, and a whole people were therefore kept at arm's length from the text. Isa 55:11 promises that God's word accomplishes what He pleases, and the promise bears on distribution as much as on preaching, since a word that reaches no one accomplishes nothing visible.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live question has changed shape. Scripture is now superabundant in the English-speaking world and little read, while hundreds of languages still have no complete Bible. Act 17:11 commends daily searching, which neither scarcity nor surfeit performs by itself. Psa 68:11 celebrates the great company of those that published it, and publishing remains the church's work in both conditions.

pos: n. (Howell Davies, c. 1716–1770, curate in Pembrokeshire, called the apostle of Pembrokeshire in the Welsh revival)
biblical_def: Howell Davies was converted under Griffith Jones, who taught him and later made him his curate, and from about 1740 he served the far southwest of Wales, where the revival had least purchase. Pembrokeshire was divided between Welsh and English speech and its gentry were hostile; Davies preached in both tongues, gathered societies at Woodstock and elsewhere, obtained a licence for the first Methodist meeting house in the county, and administered the Lord's Supper to crowds who came from across the shire. He kept his orders in the established church throughout and took the sacrament to people whom Harris as an unordained exhorter could not serve. Whitefield preached in his chapels. He worked a hard, unglamorous field for thirty years and left societies that outlasted him. 1Co 15:58 is the word over such a ministry, that your labour is not in vain in the Lord. Mat 9:37 is the condition he found there.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an apostle, in a secondary sense, as one who first plants the Christian faith in a country; and a curate, as a clergyman employed to perform the duties of another.
webster_full: APOS'TLE, n. A person deputed to execute some important business; but appropriately, a disciple of Christ commissioned to preach the gospel. The word is also applied to the first preacher of the gospel in a country.
CU'RATE, n. A clergyman employed to perform the duties of another.
SAC'RAMENT, n. The eucharist or holy communion; the solemn ordinance of the Lord's supper.
scriptures: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Mat 9:37
Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
corruption_summary: He took the ordinances to a corner of Wales the revival had hardly reached, and stayed thirty years.
corruption_paragraphs: Davies is the ordinary case, and the dictionary includes him for that reason. Revival history remembers the exceptional preachers and forgets the men who worked the difficult districts without crowds, drama or biography. 1Co 3:6 divides the labour exactly: one plants, another waters, and God gives the increase, and the verse grants no higher dignity to the planting.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is 1Co 15:58's promise, given to the stedfast and unmoveable, that their labour is not in vain in the Lord. A ministry measured against Llangeitho will always look like failure; measured against the verse, Pembrokeshire is a success. Mat 9:37 reminds us the labourers are few, which means most fields are worked by one tired man.

roots_lines: Greek auxano (G837) — to cause to grow, to give increase; 1 Corinthians 3:6.
usage: “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58) — thirty years in Pembrokeshire.
“the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37) — often one, in a hard county.
“I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6) — no rank among them.

pos: n. (Trevecca, Breconshire; Howell Harris's community from 1752 and the Countess of Huntingdon's college from 1768)
etymology: Welsh tref, a homestead or town, with the personal name Becca.
biblical_def: Trevecca was Howell Harris's family farm, and after his breach with Rowland in 1750 he gathered there a settled community — the Family — of about a hundred and twenty people living and working in common, farming with the newest methods, running a printing press and a woollen mill, worshipping several times a day. In 1768 the Countess of Huntingdon founded a college on adjoining land to train preachers for her Connexion, with Harris's help and John Fletcher as its first president; Whitefield preached at its opening. The college's early years were troubled by the Calvinist and Arminian quarrel that split Methodism, and it eventually moved to Cheshunt. The experiment in common living was not a monastery and made no vows; it was an attempt to order daily work around worship. Act 2:42 and Act 4 lie behind it. 1Co 14:40 is the caution: all things decently and in order, including enthusiasm.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a community as a society of people having common rights and privileges; and a seminary, as a place of education.
webster_full: COMMU'NITY, n. A society of people, having common rights and privileges, or common interests.
SEM'INARY, n. A place of education; any school, academy, college or university, in which young persons are instructed.
CON'NEXION, n. The act of joining, or state of being joined; union; a body of persons associated together.
scriptures: Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
corruption_summary: A Welsh farm became a commune, a printing press, a woollen mill and a preachers' college within twenty years.
corruption_paragraphs: Communities of goods recur through church history and usually fail, and the reason is worth stating fairly. Act 2 and Act 4 describe the Jerusalem church selling possessions to meet need, but the New Testament nowhere commands community of goods as a permanent order, and the epistles assume believers owning property, employing servants and supporting the poor out of it. Trevecca worked while Harris lived and dissolved after; that is the usual arc, and it is not a scandal.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lasting fruit was the college, which is 2Ti 2:2 at work: men taught so that they could teach others. Ecc 4:9 is the sober defence of the common life, that two are better than one because they have a good reward for their labour, which is a practical observation rather than a counsel of perfection. 1Co 14:40 keeps such experiments answerable to order.
roots_lines: Greek paratithemi (G3908) — to commit to one's charge; 2 Timothy 2:2.
usage: “continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship” (Act 2:42) — the Family's rule.
“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — the caution on enthusiasm.
“commit thou to faithful men” (2Ti 2:2) — the college that outlasted the commune.

pos: n. (Selina Hastings, Countess of Huntingdon, 1707–1791, patron of Calvinistic Methodism and founder of the Countess of Huntingdon's Connexion)
etymology: Countess, feminine of count, from Latin comes; Huntingdon, an English county town.
biblical_def: Selina Hastings, Countess of Huntingdon, used a peeress's rank and fortune to plant the gospel where it could not otherwise go. Converted about 1739 and widowed in 1746, she appointed Whitefield her chaplain, which under the law entitled her to maintain chapels, and she built or bought some sixty-four of them — at Bath, Brighton, Tunbridge Wells, London — places the aristocracy could attend without social cost, and where they heard the new birth preached without softening. She founded the college at Trevecca in 1768 to train preachers, sold her jewels to pay for chapels, and sent ministers to Georgia. Forced in 1781 by a consistory court to register her chapels as dissenting meeting houses, she left the established church rather than close them, and her Connexion survives. Luk 14:23 is her strategy: go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a patron as one who countenances, supports or protects; and a chapel, as a house of worship; a place of divine service.
webster_full: PA'TRON, n. One who countenances, supports or protects; a defender; an advocate. In the church of England, one who has the gift of a benefice.
CHAP'EL, n. A house for public worship; a place of divine service, subordinate to a church.
CONNEX'ION, n. A body or association of persons united; relation by blood or marriage.
scriptures: And the lord said unto the servant, Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled.
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Mat 5:16
Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness;
corruption_summary: She sold her jewels, built sixty-four chapels, and preached the new birth to duchesses who could not be reached any other way.
corruption_paragraphs: The strategy was not flattery of the great. Her chapels were built so that the nobility could hear Whitefield and Romaine without the social penalty of attending a meeting house, and what they heard was 1Co 1:23, Christ crucified, with no concession to rank. One duchess famously complained that the doctrine was monstrously insulting because it put her on a level with the common wretches that crawl the earth, which is exactly what the countess intended her to hear.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that wealth and position are stewardships to be spent, not platforms to be enjoyed. Jas 1:27 defines pure religion by visiting the afflicted and keeping unspotted from the world, and a peeress keeping unspotted in Georgian Bath was doing something difficult. Mat 5:16 ties visible works to the Father's glory, which is the right account of a woman whose chapels still stand.

pos: n. (John Elias, 1774–1841, Welsh Calvinistic Methodist preacher of Anglesey, called the Welsh Demosthenes)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Elias, the Greek form of Elijah, my God is the LORD.
biblical_def: John Elias was a Caernarvonshire farm boy who taught himself to read, walked miles to hear sermons, and became the dominant preacher in Wales for a generation. Settled on Anglesey, he preached at the great open-air associations to crowds reckoned in the tens of thousands, with a delivery contemporaries compared to thunder; a sermon of his on the woman taken in adultery is said to have emptied a fair. He drafted the Welsh Calvinistic Methodist Confession of Faith of 1823, fought the spread of Arminianism and of Thomas Jones's moderate Calvinism in the connexion, and opposed political agitation among the churches so firmly that he was nicknamed the Pope of Anglesey. The dictionary honours his doctrine and notes that his horror of change made him an obstacle in his last years. 2Ti 4:2 describes the ministry. Jude 1:3 describes the controversy. Rom 1:16 is what the crowds came to hear.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eloquence as the power of speaking with fluency and elegance, so as to persuade; and association, as a society of persons united.
webster_full: EL'OQUENCE, n. The act or art of speaking well; the power of expressing strong emotions in striking and appropriate language, so as to persuade.
ASSOCIA'TION, n. Union of persons in a company or society for some particular purpose.
ORA'TION, n. A speech or discourse, composed according to the rules of oratory, and spoken in public.

For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness;
corruption_summary: He held Welsh Calvinism together by sheer force and by the end was holding it still against its own growth.
corruption_paragraphs: Elias is a study in the cost of a watchman's temperament. Jude 1:3 requires earnest contention for the faith once delivered, and he contended; the Welsh connexion kept its Calvinism through a period when English Methodism did not, largely because of him. The same instinct, applied to questions of discipline, politics and generational change, left him by the 1830s resisting men who agreed with his doctrine and differed on prudence.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the distinction Jude draws, between the faith once delivered and everything else. A minister who defends both with the same ferocity will spend his credibility on the second and have none left for the first. 2Ti 4:2 pairs reproof and rebuke with longsuffering in a single breath, and the longsuffering is addressed to exactly this temptation.
roots_summary: Greek dunamis (G1411), power; epagonizomai (G1864), to contend earnestly; makrothumia (G3115), longsuffering.
usage: “I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ” (Rom 1:16) — preached to Anglesey's thousands.
“earnestly contend for the faith” (Jude 1:3) — and he did, at every point.
“with all longsuffering and doctrine” (2Ti 4:2) — the half he found hardest.

pos: n. (Christmas Evans, 1766–1838, Welsh Baptist preacher of Anglesey, the great imaginative preacher of Wales)
etymology: English Christmas, the mass of Christ, given as a name for his birth-day; Evans, patronymic from Evan, the Welsh John.
biblical_def: Christmas Evans was born on Christmas Day to a Cardiganshire cobbler, orphaned at nine, could not read until he was seventeen, and lost an eye in a beating from fellow farm servants. He learned letters in a Presbyterian society school, was converted, became a Baptist, and in 1792 went to Anglesey, where for thirty-four years he superintended the Baptist churches of the island on a stipend of seventeen pounds a year, travelling on a white horse and preaching sermons whose imaginative power became proverbial in Wales — the sermon on the demoniac and the one likening fallen man to a corpse on the field of Adam's battle were recited for a century. He passed through a season of doctrinal coldness under Sandemanian influence and came out of it by prayer and preaching. 1Co 1:23 names his only subject. Rom 1:16 names the power he trusted. 2Co 4:5 the rule of his pulpit: “we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines imagination as the power or faculty of the mind by which it conceives and forms ideas of things; and allegory, as a figurative sentence or discourse.
webster_full: IMAGINA'TION, n. The power or faculty of the mind by which it conceives and forms ideas of things communicated to it by the organs of sense.
AL'LEGORY, n. A figurative sentence or discourse, in which the principal subject is described by another subject resembling it in its properties and circumstances.
ILLUSTRA'TION, n. The act of explaining; explanation; elucidation; exemplification.
scriptures: But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness;
For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake.
Rom 1:16
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
corruption_summary: He could not read until seventeen and became the most vivid preacher Wales produced.
corruption_paragraphs: Evans is cited as proof that imagination belongs in the pulpit, and he is, but with the qualification he himself insisted on. His great set-pieces were expositions, not decorations: the picture always served the doctrine, and the doctrine was always Christ crucified. 2Co 4:5 states the governing rule, that preachers preach not themselves, and the test of a vivid illustration is whether the hearer remembers the Saviour or the storyteller.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Its live misuse is the sermon built from illustrations outward, where a text is attached to a story rather than a story to a text. 1Co 1:23 names the content that cannot be substituted. Psa 119:130 reminds us that it is the entrance of God's words that gives light, which Evans knew better than most, having waited seventeen years to read them.

“The entrance of thy words giveth light” (Psa 119:130) — he waited seventeen years for it.
